Does not change any leaderboard number -- v_router2 already avoids routing shape 14 (or any big-batch/big-seq shape) through the compile route for exactly this class of reason, established before this diagnosis. Value is explanatory (real mechanism for the tech report), not a new speedup.

eval.note: REAL WORKING KERNEL, CORRECT, but catastrophically slower: 0.088x (~11x SLOWER than v_router2's ~5.6x baseline for this shape/run). Took 5 real GPU attempts to get correct: (1) AttributeError on HEAD_DIM.to() -- constexpr is a plain Python int, not a tensor; (2) CompilationError -- tl.zeros((SEQ,3*D)) with 3*D=384 not a power of 2, Triton requires power-of-2 tile shapes, split into 3 separate D=128-wide GEMMs; (3) CompilationError -- 'unsupported tensor index', Triton does not support Python slice syntax on already-materialized tensor values (only on tl.load pointer expressions), restructured to compute each head's Q/K/V directly via per-head GEMMs with pointer-offset loads instead of slicing a full Q/K/V tensor; (4) OutOfResources -- needed 278528 bytes shared memory vs A100's 166912-byte limit (~67%% overshoot), fixed with explicit num_stages=1 (kernel's tl.dot calls are all single-shot, K=128 or K=32, no multi-block K-loop to pipeline anyway). ROOT CAUSE OF THE SPEED FAILURE (distinct from all the above compile bugs): grid=(1,) means this kernel runs on exactly 1 of A100's 108 SMs for the ENTIRE forward pass, with zero cross-CTA parallelism, and (after the num_stages fix) zero pipelining either. It correctly cuts launch count from ~40-60 to 1, but at the cost of using <1%% of the GPU's actual parallel hardware -- a fundamentally different bottleneck than kernel-launch overhead. Fixing this needs a genuine multi-CTA redesign (e.g. one CTA per head, or per SM-sized work-chunk with cross-CTA reduction), not further tuning of this single-CTA design. FALSIFY CONDITION TRIGGERED, unambiguously: team's own plan was 'stop if it doesn't beat reduce's 0.374ms baseline by >20%' -- this is 11x slower, not within 20%% of a win. Stopping here per the time-boxing; real, working, correctness-proven megakernel exists in the repo as documented negative-result research, not attempting a multi-CTA redesign given remaining time.

recovery: documented as negative result, not iterating further on this design

hypothesis: M2: get a real torch.profiler CUDA-kernel-level trace for shape 8 (lowest-ratio shape) instead of continuing to infer bottlenecks from opt_ms + GFLOP Roofline math -- the only method used in this repo until now.

eval.note: First real profiler trace in this repo (20 active iterations, v_router2's amp route). CUDA time breakdown: fp16 tensor-core GEMM (ampere_fp16_s16816gemm) 55.6%% -- real, expected matmul compute; dtype casting (fp32<->fp16 for autocast, aten::to/_to_copy/copy_) 17.1%% -- a REAL, previously-unmeasured overhead specific to mixing fp32 storage with fp16 compute; Triton AddNorm (T7) 6.75%%; unfused residual-add (the post-FFN one, not covered by T7's fusion) 6.05%%; flash attention (fires here, fp16-eligible) 6.02%%; unfused LayerNorm (norm1, also not covered by T7) 5.81%%; GELU 1.92%%. KEY IMPLICATION FOR T10: T10's kernel forces input_precision="ieee" (full fp32 accumulation) uniformly across all shapes for correctness safety. Shape 8's actual bottleneck under the CURRENT best route (amp) is 55.6%% fp16 tensor-core GEMM + 17.1%% casting overhead -- T10 in fp32 form gets neither the fp16 tensor-core throughput nor any casting reduction on this shape, so its 0.84x regression there is not just 'needs autotuning', it's solving a different problem than what's actually slow. T10 (fp32) is structurally a better fit for the shapes that do NOT route to amp (where the baseline is already fp32 and T10's savings are real bandwidth/launch reduction, not competing against fp16 tensor cores it doesn't use).

Most OTHER shapes got slightly WORSE than the original hand-picked (64,64,32) default: shape 1 1.56x (was 1.73x), shape 9 1.41x (was 1.56x), shape 13 4.25x (was 4.53x). Only shapes 5/6/11 improved. For the other shapes, the original default was already close to a local optimum; Triton's own internal autotuning benchmark (a separate pass with its own warmup/cache state) picked configs that don't quite transfer to bench_harness's official measurement protocol. Real, correct, informative negative result for the AUTOTUNING specifically -- T10 the kernel itself remains real and correct, wins on most shapes either way; the right next fix for shape 8 is giving T10 an fp16-compute mode (mirroring what amp actually needs), not more block-size search.

eval.note: 13/13 correct, max_abs<=0.0013 (well inside the 0.002 budget) -- the correctness risk flagged at write-time (an earlier blanket fp16 cast this session had failed 11/12 shapes) did NOT materialize this time. RESULT: fp16 genuinely improved shape 8 off T10-fp32's 0.83x floor (now 1.31x standalone-vs-plain-best.py), a real fix for the precision-mismatch diagnosis -- but it is still BELOW v_router2's current amp route on all 3 shapes that matter (6: 2.24x vs 3.29x, 8: 1.31x vs 1.74x, 13: 4.38x vs 11.66x). A hand-written Triton fp16 GEMM cannot beat cuBLASLt's tensor-core GEMM at these sizes. Consistent with M2's profiler breakdown: GELU is only 1.92% of shape 8's CUDA time, so once the 55.6% GEMM time is treated as fixed cost (any correct fp16 GEMM has to do that work), fusion has almost no addressable overhead left to win on. DECISION: do not route T10 (fp32 or fp16) to shapes #6/#8/#13 -- leave amp's plain nn.Linear+GELU there. T10-fp32 remains a real win for the other 10 (non-amp) shapes, unaffected by this finding. Closing the T10-vs-shape-8 thread: beating cuBLASLt's own GEMM is out of scope for a hand-rolled fusion kernel; a real fix would need a different algorithm or library, not more fusion.

hypothesis: K4 (docs/research-agent-findings.md): audit whether v_router2's compile/reduce-overhead routes get static CUDA-graph parameter addresses, or silently pay a hidden per-call D2D-copy tax -- and whether running several compile/reduce shapes in one process (what a real sweep does) causes cudagraph pool interference that could explain S2's still-open 'reduce wins in isolation, regresses in the full sweep' mystery.

eval.note: Used torch._logging.set_logs(cudagraphs=True, recompiles=True) -- PyTorch's own internal diagnostic, not inference. Isolated (each shape its own process): 0 recompiles, 0 allocator checkpoints, clean single cudagraph-tree recording each. Back-to-back in one process (real-sweep shape): 4 Dynamo recompiles + 5 CUDA-caching-allocator checkpoint/restores across just 6 shapes. ROOT CAUSE TRACED: _CompileTransformerBase._forward_impl (v_router2.py:337) is one shared class method, torch.compile'd fresh per instance -- Dynamo's guard cache keys on the shared code object, not per-instance. v_router2's own S1-motivated per-route allow_tf32 toggle (v_router2.py:520-535, intentional, already documented) is a Dynamo-tracked GLOBAL_STATE guard: every switch into/out of a 'compile'-routed shape invalidates prior cache entries -- confirmed directly in the log (shape 3's first call recompiled specifically for 'GLOBAL_STATE changed: allow_tf32' against both shape 1 and shape 2's cached entries). NOT the mechanism K4 originally guessed: zero skip/alias/copy warnings anywhere, cudagraph capture succeeded cleanly every time -- non-static-address D2D-copy tax was not observed. WHY THIS DOESN'T EXPLAIN S2: warmup_model() (torch_transformer_benchmark.py:463, called once per shape before that shape's own benchmark_once) runs all compilation/recompilation inside the UNTIMED warmup loop, synced before the timed CUDA-event loop starts -- structurally this cost inflates total sweep wall-clock time but cannot leak into the per-shape speedup numbers that populate the leaderboard. S2 REMAINS OPEN. One real, not-yet-tested lead surfaced: allocator-checkpoint state accumulates across the one-process run (5 checkpoints for 6 shapes) -- could plausibly slow cudagraph pool allocation/replay for shapes appearing LATER in a 13-shape sweep (S2's #9/#10 come after 8 other shapes' instances), but this run only captured log events, not actual per-call latency, so that's a hypothesis for a follow-up, not a finding.

eval.note: job 778997. 10/10 correct, but WORSE than the non-persistent K1a on every single shape -- geomean 0.55x, several shapes actively slower than baseline (shape1 0.27x, shape5 0.22x, shape9 0.25x).
